label: MODEL ESTIMATE: typical values for planning, not measurements
source: Typical estimates only. Frequency scaling follows free-space loss, 20*log10(f/2.4 GHz). Material attenuation values are rounded typical figures in the range reported by ITU-R P.2040 (building material properties) and published indoor measurements (for example NIST and vendor site-survey guides). Real walls vary by thickness, moisture, reinforcement and construction, so calibrate with a site survey before relying on them. Rate tables are typical 802.11n/ac/ax minimum-sensitivity style figures for one spatial stream, not vendor guarantees.

glass.label: Glass
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
glass.notes: Plain single or double glazing. Low-emissivity or metal-coated glass can exceed 20 dB and is not covered, add it as a custom material.

drywall.label: Drywall
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
drywall.notes: Single or double plasterboard on studs. Insulation or foil backing raises the loss.

wood.label: Wood
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
wood.notes: Solid timber or timber stud partitions. Thickness and moisture content change the loss.

brick.label: Brick
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
brick.notes: Single-leaf brick or block wall. Plaster, cavities and thickness move the loss within the range.

concrete.label: Concrete
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
concrete.notes: Plain concrete or dense block wall without dense reinforcement.

metal.label: Metal
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
metal.notes: Sheet metal, lift shafts, foil-backed panels. Close to total blockage, the measured loss is set by leakage at gaps and edges.

reinforced_concrete.label: Reinforced concrete
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
reinforced_concrete.notes: Concrete with steel reinforcement. The rebar mesh spacing relative to the wavelength dominates and varies a lot, so the range is wide.

stone.label: Stone
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
stone.notes: Natural stone masonry. Thickness and porosity vary widely.

plaster.label: Plaster
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
plaster.notes: Plaster or render on lath or thin masonry backing. A wire mesh or metal lath backing raises the loss well above the typical value.

insulation.label: Insulation
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
insulation.notes: Mineral wool or foam insulation panel without a metal facing. Foil-faced insulation behaves like a thin metal sheet and loses much more, so model it with the metal material.

office_partition.label: Office partition
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
office_partition.notes: Modular office partition of fabric or laminate panels on a light frame, typically 1 to 2 m high screens up to full-height glazed partitions. Full-height steel-framed partitions lose more.

industrial_wall.label: Industrial wall
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
industrial_wall.notes: Thick concrete block, precast panel or corrugated steel cladding of a factory or warehouse. The range is wide because cladding, racking and stored goods change the loss; use the metal material for a solid steel sheet.

flooring.label: Flooring
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
ITU-R P.1238 (indoor propagation, floor penetration loss) for the floor-loss context
flooring.notes: Light timber or composite floor build-up. The 2D engine applies floors as a fixed floor_loss_db per floor crossed, this entry is a reference for that value and for a future 3D model. Selecting it for a wall models a thin partition.

roofing.label: Roofing
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
ITU-R P.1238 (indoor propagation, floor penetration loss) for the floor-loss context
roofing.notes: Tiles or sheet over timber, no metal foil. Foil-backed or metal roofing is much higher. The 2D engine has no roof, this entry is a reference for a future 3D model. Selecting it for a wall models a thin partition.

wifi_standards.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: PHY rates follow the IEEE 802.11 OFDM formula, minimum-SNR values are typical planning figures
wifi_standards.source: PHY rate = data subcarriers x bits per subcarrier x coding rate x spatial streams / symbol time (IEEE 802.11n-2009 clause 20, 802.11ac-2013 clause 21, 802.11ax-2021 clause 27, 802.11be-2024 clause 36). Data subcarrier counts and symbol times are the per-standard OFDM numerology of those clauses. Minimum-SNR per MCS are rounded typical planning figures (the standards normative receiver minimum sensitivity is a dBm value per MCS, not an SNR), not vendor guarantees. 802.11ac MCS 9 is not defined for every width and stream count, this model ignores that restriction.

mlo.label: CAPACITY MODEL, not a measurement: Multi-Link Operation (IEEE 802.11be-2024) aggregates the rates of the links, real gains depend on the client, the MLO mode and the traffic

interference.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: SINR from co-channel and adjacent-channel interference, a planning aid
interference.source: Thermal noise density -174 dBm/Hz at 290 K (kT, Johnson-Nyquist). Channel centres follow the IEEE 802.11 channel numbering (centre MHz = base + 5 x channel). The adjacent-channel rejection table is rounded from the IEEE 802.11 OFDM transmit spectrum mask for 20 MHz (about -20 dBr at 11 MHz, -28 dBr at 20 MHz and -40 dBr at 30 MHz from the centre), applied to the gap between the edges of the two occupied bandwidths. The noise figure and the activity factor are planning assumptions.

antenna.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: horizontal antenna pattern in the plan plane, no elevation, polarisation or near-field effects
antenna.source: The sector pattern is the 3GPP TR 36.814 horizontal pattern A(phi) = -min(12 (phi / phi_3dB)^2, A_m), phi_3dB the 3 dB beamwidth and A_m the front-to-back ratio. Azimuth 0 points along +x (east) and increases towards +y (south, clockwise on the plan).

external_sources.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: non-WiFi and neighbouring interference sources, planning assumptions, not measurements
external_sources.source: Each source is a spectrally flat emitter: its power is spread evenly over width_mhz around centre_mhz and the share that lands inside the victim receive band is overlap / width_mhz, scaled by duty_cycle. Microwave oven: a magnetron oven runs from half-wave rectified mains and radiates during about half of each mains cycle (the commonly cited 50 percent duty cycle), around 2.45 GHz inside the 2.4 to 2.5 GHz ISM band; the 50 MHz width and the 10 dBm effective leakage level are planning assumptions (ovens are limited by leakage rules, FCC 21 CFR 1030.10 and IEC 60335-2-25, not by a radiated spectrum mask). Bluetooth: 79 channels of 1 MHz from 2402 to 2480 MHz (Bluetooth Core Specification, BR/EDR hopping), class 2 maximum 2.5 mW (4 dBm); hopping is modelled as the average spread over the 78 MHz hop set, so a 20 MHz WiFi channel sees about 20/78 of the power; the duty cycle is a planning assumption for a connected audio or data link. Neighbour WiFi: a co-located network is treated like an AP of this project (same channel coupling and rejection table) with its own duty_cycle, a planning assumption for typical residential traffic. Non-WiFi sources have no adjacent-channel skirt.

reliability.label: ESTIMATE: airtime, latency and packet loss follow from SINR through an assumed PER curve. There is no standard formula, treat the numbers as indications, not measurements
reliability.source: PER(sinr) is a logistic curve 1 / (1 + exp((sinr - min_snr) / per_scale_db + ln((1 - per_at_min_snr) / per_at_min_snr))) around the MCS minimum SNR, so PER equals per_at_min_snr at that SNR. The 10 percent point follows the IEEE 802.11 receiver minimum sensitivity definition (PER 10 percent for a 1000 octet PSDU). per_scale_db sets how fast PER falls, a planning assumption. The MCS is the highest one the SINR supports. Packets are retried up to retry_limit times (IEEE 802.11 dot11ShortRetryLimit default 7), so the loss after retries is PER^(retry_limit + 1) and the mean transmissions are the sum of PER^k for k up to retry_limit. Latency = base_latency_ms + retries x retry_penalty_ms + busy / (1 - busy) x medium_wait_ms, with busy the share of time the serving AP hears non-WiFi or neighbour sources above the carrier sense level. base_latency_ms, retry_penalty_ms and medium_wait_ms are planning assumptions. Airtime is the share of the channel one client at the demand rate needs: demand / (PHY rate x MAC efficiency x (1 - PER) x (1 - busy)).

voids.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: stairwell and atrium openings reduce the floor loss locally, a planning approximation of the 2D plan
voids.source: A void is an optional polygon or rectangle on a floor where the slab is open (stairwell, lift shaft, atrium). The 2D model has no slab geometry, so the floor loss between two floors is scaled down by open_end_reduction for every end of the path (the AP, the receiver) that lies inside a void on its own floor. With both ends inside a void the floor loss is removed (reduction capped at 1). open_end_reduction is a planning assumption; real stairwells with doors or balustrades differ.

spectrum.label: ESTIMATE: channel congestion from the access points and sources of the project, a planning aid, not a scan of the air
spectrum.source: Congestion of a channel is the sum over every AP and source in the project of coupling x duty cycle, where coupling is the share of the source power that lands in the candidate channel (interference.rejection_table for WiFi, spectral overlap for non-WiFi sources). It ignores distance, so it counts every source as if heard. APs use interference.activity_factor as duty cycle. Levels are thresholds on the congestion value, planning assumptions. On 2.4 GHz only the non-overlapping channels in preferred_channels are suggested.

decay.label: ESTIMATE: signal decay along a ray from an AP, from the same propagation model as the coverage map

roaming.label: ESTIMATE: exact per-cell roaming data from the strongest and second strongest AP, the blend is a planning aid, not a client roaming simulation
roaming.source: Per cell: the strongest AP, the second AP, the margin between them and a zone. Zone handoff: both APs at least analytics.roam_min_dbm and the margin at most analytics.roam_margin_db. Zone overlap: a second AP at least analytics.overlap_min_dbm within analytics.overlap_margin_db of the strongest. Else single. Blend is the share of the cell notionally served by the strongest AP: 50 percent at zero margin rising linearly to 100 percent at analytics.roam_margin_db. Client roaming thresholds and stickiness are not modelled.

scoring.label: Optimisation score, a weighted sum of estimates, higher is better. Weights are planning preferences, not physics.

planner.label: Smart WiFi Planner settings. Recommendations are model estimates, confidence expresses model sensitivity, not real-world accuracy.

planner_modes.label: ESTIMATE: planning aids built on the propagation model, typical values, not measurements
